title: FRM Current Issues, Lesson 4: AI and machine learning in risk management
subtitle: Better predictions, worse explanations - and the regulator wants both
whyItMatters: Machine learning has already moved into credit scoring, fraud detection and trade surveillance. But risk management carries a constraint many other fields do not: the decision has to be explainable to the customer and to the regulator.
openingQuestion: What is the central trade-off in putting a machine learning model into a credit decision?
openingOptions: More accurate predictions, but no clear reason why one file was declined
Lower running costs, but a longer processing time on every application
More applications handled, but only usable for corporate customers
Lower credit risk, but higher liquidity risk for the bank
explanation: A linear model tells you how much each variable contributed; a deep non-linear model has no such tidy answer. The problem is that rules in many countries require a stated reason for declining credit - so higher accuracy does not automatically mean the model can be used.

diagram.label: Machine learning catches non-linear relationships traditional models miss
In exchange: it is hard to trace why the decision came out that way
New risks: bias in the training data, model drift
The model governance framework has to stretch to cover both

realWorldExample.company: Why bias in training data is a legal risk, not just a technical one
realWorldExample.description: A model learns from past decisions, so it learns the biases those decisions carried. If the historical data reflects a group of customers being declined more often than they should have been, the model reproduces exactly that pattern and makes it more efficient. What makes it dangerous is that it needs no sensitive variable to do so - proxies such as where someone lives or how they spend are already enough.

quiz.question: What does model drift mean?
options: The model is retrained so often that its output becomes unstable over time
The model runs slower over time as stored data volume grows
Model parameters get altered by a technical fault during storage
The link between inputs and outcomes shifts, so the model decays
quiz.explanation: As the world changes, the relationship the model learned from the past goes stale - customer behaviour moves, the economic cycle turns. That is why monitoring performance after deployment matters as much as validating before it. Retraining frequency, compute load and storage faults are all real operational problems, but none of them is drift: drift happens even when the code, the parameters and the infrastructure are untouched, because the population being scored is no longer the population the model learned from.

quiz.question: Why can a machine learning model reproduce bias without using any sensitive variable?
options: Because proxies such as where someone lives correlate tightly with it
Because ML algorithms are designed to segment customers demographically
Because training data must always carry full demographic information
Because a model cannot run without basic demographic variables present
quiz.explanation: Dropping a sensitive variable from the inputs does not remove the information, because it is spread across the others: postcode, spending pattern, the device used to apply. A non-linear model with hundreds of features recombines them and rebuilds the deleted variable with high accuracy. That is why fairness testing has to measure outcomes by group rather than stop at auditing the input list - and why no algorithm needs to be designed to segment demographically for the effect to show up.

quiz.question: Why does systemic risk rise as more institutions use the same model?
options: Because model vendors raise prices as their customer base grows
Because many institutions react identically to the same signal
Because a shared model runs slower as the compute estate is strained
Because regulators forbid several firms using one model vendor
quiz.explanation: This is herding in a new form. When institutions run similar models over similar data, they see the sell signal at the same moment - individually rational behaviour that produces a common drawdown for everyone. The channel is the shared model rather than any shared instruction, which is what makes it a systemic issue rather than a vendor pricing issue. Regulators do not ban concentration among model vendors, and infrastructure load has nothing to do with correlated positions.

quiz.question: Why are machine learning models in credit held to a far higher explainability standard than models used in marketing?
options: Because credit data holds more sensitive variables than shopping data
Because credit models are usually less accurate than marketing models
Because the rules require a specific reason when credit is declined
Because credit models need regulatory approval before deployment
quiz.explanation: This is a legal constraint rather than a technical preference: someone refused credit has the right to know why. A model that is more accurate but cannot state a reason still cannot be used at that step, which is what makes the accuracy-versus-explainability trade-off real rather than academic. Marketing carries no equivalent duty, so the same technique is deployable there without argument. Prior approval exists in some regimes but not everywhere, and it is not what forces explainability.

quiz.question: Why watch the distribution of the input data rather than only the model's accuracy?
options: Because a change in the inputs stops the model working altogether
Because accuracy can only be measured months after the outcome
Because the input mix caps how many variables a model may use
Input drifting away from training data is the earlier signal
quiz.explanation: For a credit model the true outcome is only known months later, by which point the loss has already been booked. Watching the input distribution drift is the only early signal available today, and it needs no realised labels at all. The second option states something true about accuracy but draws the wrong conclusion from it - the point is not that accuracy is hard to compute, but that it is a lagging indicator. Changed inputs do not stop a model running; they make it run confidently on a population it has never seen.

practicePrompt.question: A machine learning credit scorecard has held 88% accuracy for six months, but the share of self-employed applicants in the incoming flow has gone from 5% to 30%. What needs doing?
options: Watch the input distribution: drift arrives before accuracy falls
Nothing is needed, since accuracy held at 88% for six months
Retrain immediately using the entire historical data set
Drop occupation from the model to avoid bias against this group
practicePrompt.explanation: Accuracy is measured on files that already have an outcome, meaning loans disbursed months ago, when the incoming flow still looked like the training data. It is a lagging indicator. The input distribution can be measured today, and a group moving from 5% to 30% means the model is scoring a different population from the one it learned - accuracy will fall, it simply has not been observed yet. Dropping occupation solves nothing: a machine learning model rebuilds bias through correlated variables without needing any sensitive one, so removing the variable removes only your ability to see the bias, not the bias itself.

keyTakeaways: The central trade-off: higher accuracy bought with lower explainability
The model learns the biases in the historical data, even with no sensitive variable present
Drift makes post-deployment monitoring as important as pre-deployment validation
Widely shared models increase herding and systemic risk

summary.keyIdea: Machine learning creates no entirely new category of risk, but it makes model risk heavier and far harder to see
summary.commonMistake: Judging a model only on test-set accuracy, ignoring explainability and the fairness of its outcomes
summary.action: For every machine learning model that feeds a decision, ask: if the customer asks why they were declined, what do we say?

application.title: Questions to put to every model
application.message: Three are enough to expose most of the problems: which period did the model learn from, do outcomes differ across customer groups, and who is accountable when it is wrong.
application.secondary: All three apply equally to traditional models and to machine learning ones.

sections.text: Machine learning arriving in finance brought no risk category that had never existed. It took a known one - model risk - and made it heavier and harder to see.

items: Explainability: rules in many countries require a stated reason for declining credit
Bias: the model learns the unfair patterns already sitting in historical data
Drift: relationships learned from the past go stale as the world moves

sections.label: Removing sensitive variables is not enough for fairness
sections.text: Information about gender or ethnic group is spread across dozens of other variables - where someone lives, how they spend, which device they applied from. Fairness testing therefore has to measure the gap in outcomes by group rather than stop at auditing the input list.

When many institutions buy models from the same handful of vendors and train them on similar data, they start reacting the same way to the same signal. This is herding - the thing that has turned many isolated shocks into shared crises - now with an additional transmission channel.
Why taking the sensitive variables out solves nothing

A credit scorecard is not allowed to use gender or ethnicity - and deleting those two columns is the easiest step available, as well as the least effective. Postcode, the type of phone used to apply, the hour of day the borrower pressed the button, the merchant names that keep appearing on the statement: each variable correlates only weakly with a demographic group, but a non-linear model with a few hundred features combines them and reconstructs the deleted variable with high accuracy. That is why fairness testing has to measure OUTCOMES by group rather than audit the list of inputs.

sections.title: Three questions the regulator will ask, and what must be ready
sections.subtitle: All answerable before deployment, or not answerable at all

concepts.def: You must be able to state a specific reason for each decision. A gradient-boosted tree with thousands of splits cannot do that on its own, so an explanation layer is needed - and that explanation has to match the actual decision, not be a generic sentence pasted on afterwards.
Measure approval rates and error rates by group rather than inspecting the variable list. A model that is clean on inputs can still be visibly skewed on outputs.

Machine learning decays faster than regression when behaviour changes, because it hugs the training data more closely. Monitor drift in the input distribution, not just accuracy - accuracy only falls after the damage has been done.

lines: A model that cannot be explained is a model that cannot be challenged.
Next lesson: the category of risk for which no historical data holds a precedent.
